routes.label: Shift and subtract finite partial sums

question: The limiting sum of the infinite series \[ \frac1{10}+\frac2{10^2}+\frac3{10^3}+\cdots, \] whose \(n\)th term is \(\frac{n}{10^n},\) is:
solution:
Dividing the sum by \(10\) shifts its terms so that equal denominators line up. Subtraction then changes the consecutive numerators into differences of \(1\). Work first with finite sums so that the last term is retained.

For a positive integer \(N\), let
\[
S_N=\frac1{10}+\frac2{10^2}+\cdots+\frac N{10^N}.
\]
Subtracting \(S_N/10\) gives
\[
\frac9{10}S_N
=\frac1{10}+\frac1{10^2}+\cdots+\frac1{10^N}
-\frac N{10^{N+1}}.
\]
Indeed, at denominator \(10^k\) for \(2\leq k\leq N\), the numerator becomes \(k-(k-1)=1\); the shifted sum contributes the final negative term.

The geometric sum on the right has first term \(1/10\) and ratio \(1/10\), so its limit is
\[
\frac{1/10}{1-1/10}=\frac19.
\]
To check the remaining endpoint, write \(a_N=N/10^{N+1}\). For \(N\geq1\),
\[
\frac{a_{N+1}}{a_N}
=\frac{N+1}{10N}\leq\frac15.
\]
Thus \(0<a_N\leq\frac1{100}(\frac15)^{N-1}\), which tends to \(0\). The identity for \(S_N\) therefore proves that the original series converges. Its sum \(S\) satisfies
\[
\frac9{10}S=\frac19,
\qquad S=\frac{10}{81}.
\]
The limiting sum is \(\frac{10}{81}\), choice B.
